newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt eyes highs, seen shrugging off losses.
newsitem.headline: German debt eyes highs, seen shrugging off losses.

text.p: German debt slipped in early trading on Thursday but losses were seen to be limited as Bunds have shown remarkable resilience in recent sessions and were thus tapped to test new highs not lows, dealers said.

"After Bunds underperformed most other markets and they are still considered to be one of the cheapest assets, I think it is rather likely they will move higher soon," said a Duesseldorf-based dealer.
By 0747 GMT the September Bund futures contract was trading down four basis points at 101.68, having moved between 101.69 and 101.57 since the opening.
At the same time the 10-year cash bond was trading at 102.21 compared with Wednesday's close of 102.30.

Early losses were largely attributed to U.S. Treasury market weakness where a late-session selling wave pushed prices lower. One reason given for the U.S. market losses was that a central bank was said to have sold $1 billion in 10-year notes.
But German dealers were convinced the negative knock-on effect from Wednesday's Treasury market losses would be short-lived, with futures testing the old high of 101.87 soon.
"The market is just so well supported that we think it will go higher before it goes lower," added another dealer.
For Thursday, dealers put the day's range between 101.50 and 101.85, with dealers unsure whether enough energy could be mustered to break and hold above old highs.
"We are seeing a lack of real investors in the market," lamented one dealer, noting this would make it difficult to generate sufficient momentum for any serious move.
On the other hand another dealer added that low volumes could also be seen to benefit any potential upward move.
"With such low volumes, it will only take a little bit of buying to push the market quite a bit higher," another dealer added.

Dealers were particularly interested in comments made by Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen late on Wednesday that he would not rule out another German interest rate cut, even though he did not see it.
The Bundesbank is holding its regular meeting on Thursday.
"These comments show the Bundesbank is very eager to keep rate cut hopes alive," a dealer said.

This might be crucially important in the run-up to Germany's planned 30-year bond issue, the first time Bonn has tapped the extra-long end of the bond market since late 1993, dealers said, noting the issue could signal an end to easing.

If the government agrees to lock into current rates for 30-years it might signal Bonn no longer expects a rate cut, dealers said. But the government has said it plans to issue the 30-year bond as part of plans to allow bond stripping where the principal and interest can be traded separately.
The issue is expected next week and is slated to total no more than 10 billion marks.
